claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are RNA molecules that catalyze the cleavage of their own phosphodiester backbones.
source: Self-cleaving ribozymes are RNA molecules that catalyze the cleavage of their own phosphodiester backbones.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract that defines what self-cleaving ribozymes are.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are found in all domains of life.
source: These ribozymes are found in all domains of life and are also a tool for biotechnical and synthetic biology applications.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about the distribution of self-cleaving ribozymes.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are a tool for biotechnical and synthetic biology applications.
source: These ribozymes are found in all domains of life and are also a tool for biotechnical and synthetic biology applications.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about the applications of self-cleaving ribozymes.

claim: The study determined the relative activity for every possible single and double mutant of five self-cleaving ribozymes using a high-throughput experimental approach.
source: Here, we used a high-throughput experimental approach to determine the relative activity for every possible single and double mutant of five self-cleaving ribozymes.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and scope of the study, which is supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study comprehensively identified non-additive effects between pairs of mutations (epistasis) for all five ribozymes.
source: From this data, we comprehensively identified non-additive effects between pairs of mutations (epistasis) for all five ribozymes.
evidence: This is supported by the epistasis calculations and analyses presented throughout the results section.

claim: Heatmap-based visualization of the data revealed patterns indicating structural features of the ribozymes including paired regions, unpaired loops, non-canonical structures, and tertiary structural contacts.
source: Heatmap-based visualization of the data revealed patterns indicating structural features of the ribozymes including paired regions, unpaired loops, non-canonical structures, and tertiary structural contacts.
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap figures (Figures 1-5) and the analysis of structural features throughout the results section.

claim: The data revealed signatures of functionally critical nucleotides involved in catalysis.
source: The data also revealed signatures of functionally critical nucleotides involved in catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of catalytic residues presented in the results section.

claim: Machine learning approaches have made considerable advancements in predicting an RNA structure from a sequence.
source: Recently, machine learning approaches have made considerable advancements in predicting an RNA structure from a sequence.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature on machine learning approaches for RNA structure prediction.

claim: Machine learning approaches for RNA structure prediction rely heavily on crystal structures of RNA molecules and sequence conservation of homologs.
source: However, these approaches rely heavily on crystal structures of RNA molecules and sequence conservation of homologs, both of which are limited for RNA molecules compared to proteins (Calonaci et al., 2020; Townshend et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant literature discussing the limitations of current machine learning approaches.

claim: Crystal structures and sequence conservation data are more limited for RNA molecules compared to proteins.
source: However, these approaches rely heavily on crystal structures of RNA molecules and sequence conservation of homologs, both of which are limited for RNA molecules compared to proteins (Calonaci et al., 2020; Townshend et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature discussing the relative availability of structural data for RNA versus proteins.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes were first discovered in viruses and viroids.
source: They were first discovered in viruses and viroids, but numerous families of self-cleaving ribozymes have since been discovered in all domains of life (Prody et al., 1986).
evidence: This historical statement is supported by a citation to the original discovery.

claim: Numerous families of self-cleaving ribozymes have been discovered in all domains of life.
source: They were first discovered in viruses and viroids, but numerous families of self-cleaving ribozymes have since been discovered in all domains of life (Prody et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about the widespread distribution of self-cleaving ribozymes.

claim: The CPEB3 ribozyme was discovered in the human genome and found to be highly conserved in mammals.
source: The CPEB3 ribozyme, for example, was discovered in the human genome and found to be highly conserved in mammals (Bendixsen et al., 2021; Salehi-Ashtiani et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that discovered and characterized the CPEB3 ribozyme.

claim: Hammerhead and twister ribozymes are found broadly distributed across eukaryotic and prokaryotic genomes.
source: Other self-cleaving ribozymes, such as the hammerhead and twister ribozymes, are found broadly distributed across eukaryotic and prokaryotic genomes (Perreault et al., 2011; Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies documenting the distribution of these ribozymes.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes have been used for several bioengineering applications.
source: In addition to being widespread across the tree of life, self-cleaving ribozymes have also been used for several bioengineering applications (Liang et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2021; Wei and Smolke, 2015; Zhong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating bioengineering applications.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes are being combined with aptamers to develop synthetic gene regulatory devices.
source: For example, self-cleaving ribozymes are being combined with aptamers to develop synthetic gene regulatory devices, which have biotechnical and biomedical applications where ligand-dependent control of gene expression is desired (Kobori et al., 2017; Kobori et al., 2015; Stifel et al., 2019; Townshend et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies developing synthetic gene regulatory devices.

claim: Most self-cleaving ribozymes are fairly small (<200 nt).
source: Most self-cleaving ribozymes are fairly small (<200 nt), and genetic variants can be made by chemical synthesis of a single DNA oligonucleotide that is then used as a template for in vitro transcription.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the typical size range of self-cleaving ribozymes.

claim: The self-cleavage activity of ribozymes requires a precise three-dimensional structure.
source: The self-cleavage activity of the ribozyme requires a precise three-dimensional structure, and therefore activity can be used as a sensitive indirect readout of native structure.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the relationship between RNA structure and function.

claim: Activity can be used as a sensitive indirect readout of native structure in ribozymes.
source: The self-cleavage activity of the ribozyme requires a precise three-dimensional structure, and therefore activity can be used as a sensitive indirect readout of native structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between structure and function in ribozymes.

claim: Mutations that disrupt the native structure are detected as reduced activity compared to the unmutated 'wild-type' ribozyme.
source: Mutations that disrupt the native structure are detected as reduced activity compared to the unmutated 'wild-type' ribozyme.
evidence: This is based on the principle that structural disruption leads to functional impairment.

claim: Several methods have been developed to enable the detection of ribozyme function by high-throughput sequencing of biochemical reactions.
source: Several methods have been developed to enable the detection of ribozyme function by high-throughput sequencing of biochemical reactions (Bendixsen et al., 2019; Hayden, 2016; Kobori and Yokobayashi, 2016; Shen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies developing high-throughput sequencing methods for ribozyme analysis.

claim: For self-cleaving ribozymes, each read from the data reports both the mutations and whether or not that molecule was reacted (cleaved) or unreacted (uncleaved).
source: For self-cleaving ribozymes, each read from the data reports both the mutations and whether or not that molecule was reacted (cleaved) or unreacted (uncleaved).
evidence: This describes the nature of the sequencing data obtained from the experimental approach.

claim: Pairwise epistasis measures deviations in the mutational effects of double mutants relative to the effects of each individual mutation (assuming an additive model of mutational effects).
source: In this context, it can be useful to calculate pairwise epistasis, which measures deviations in the mutational effects of double mutants relative to the effects of each individual mutation (assuming an additive model of mutational effects).
evidence: This is a definitional statement explaining what pairwise epistasis measures.

claim: In the case of a base pair, each single mutation would disrupt the base-pairing interaction, destabilizing the catalytically active RNA structure and reducing activity.
source: For example, in the case of a base pair, each single mutation would disrupt the base-pairing interaction, destabilizing the catalytically active RNA structure and reducing activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about how mutations affect base pairing and RNA structure.

claim: If two mutants together restore a base pair, the RA of the double mutant would have much higher activity than expected from the additive effects of the individual mutations (positive epistasis).
source: However, if two mutants together restore a base pair, the RA of the double mutant would have much higher activity than expected from the additive effects of the individual mutations (positive epistasis).
evidence: This is an inference based on the principle of compensatory mutations in base pairs.

claim: Double mutants at non-paired nucleotides tend to have a more reduced activity than expected from each individual mutation (negative epistasis).
source: In contrast to paired nucleotides, double mutants at non-paired nucleotides tend to have a more reduced activity than expected from each individual mutation (negative epistasis) (Bendixsen et al., 2017; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies observing this pattern.

claim: The ribozymes studied include a mammalian CPEB3 ribozyme, a hepatitis delta virus (HDV) ribozyme, a twister ribozyme from Oryza sativa, a hairpin ribozyme derived from the satellite RNA from tobacco ringspot virus, and a hammerhead ribozyme.
source: The ribozymes studied include a mammalian CPEB3 ribozyme, a hepatitis delta virus (HDV) ribozyme, a twister ribozyme from Oryza sativa, a hairpin ribozyme derived from the satellite RNA from tobacco ringspot virus, and a hammerhead ribozyme (Bendixsen et al., 2021; Burke and Greathouse, 2005; Chadalavada et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2014; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the specific ribozymes studied, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: For each reference ribozyme, a single DNA oligo template library was synthesized with 97% wild-type nucleotides at each position, and 1% of each of the three other nucleotides.
source: For each reference ribozyme, a single DNA oligo template library was synthesized with 97% wild-type nucleotides at each position, and 1% of each of the three other nucleotides.
evidence: This describes the mutagenesis strategy used in the study.

claim: This mutagenesis strategy was expected to produce all possible single and double mutants, as well as a random sampling of combinations of three or more mutations.
source: This mutagenesis strategy was expected to produce all possible single and double mutants, as well as a random sampling of combinations of three or more mutations.
evidence: This is an inference about the expected outcome of the mutagenesis strategy.

claim: All ribozyme constructs studied cleave near the 5′-end of the RNA.
source: All ribozyme constructs studied cleave near the 5′-end of the RNA, and a template switching reverse transcription protocol was used to append a common primer binding site to both cleaved and uncleaved molecules.
evidence: This describes a common feature of the ribozyme constructs used in the study.

claim: Many paired regions showed an anti-diagonal line of high-activity double mutant variants with strong positive epistasis.
source: In this heatmap layout, many paired regions showed an anti-diagonal line of high-activity double mutant variants with strong positive epistasis (Figures 1—5, insets, red to blue plots).
evidence: This observation is supported by the heatmap visualizations in Figures 1-5.

claim: Pairs of mutations off the anti-diagonal tended to show negative or non-positive epistasis.
source: In addition, pairs of mutations off the anti-diagonal tended to show negative or non-positive epistasis.
evidence: This observation is supported by the epistasis data shown in the heatmaps.

claim: Pseudoknot elements that involve Watson-Crick base pairs showed the pattern of positive epistasis on the anti-diagonal.
source: Pseudoknot elements that involve Watson-Crick base pairs also showed this pattern, including the single base pair T1 element in CPEB3 (Figure 1) and the two base pair T1 element in HDV (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: For all ribozymes, disrupting two base pairs resulted in negative epistasis (mean of distribution).
source: For all ribozymes, the analysis revealed a clear trend. On average, disrupting two base pairs resulted in negative epistasis (mean of distribution), disrupting one base pair shifted the distribution toward more positive epistasis values, and the highest epistasis values (mean and max) were found for double mutants that result in zero disrupted base pairs because the two mutations together create a new Watson-Crick or GU Wobble pair.
evidence: This is supported by the violin plot analysis shown in Figures 1-5, panel C.

claim: Disrupting one base pair shifted the distribution toward more positive epistasis values.
source: For all ribozymes, the analysis revealed a clear trend. On average, disrupting two base pairs resulted in negative epistasis (mean of distribution), disrupting one base pair shifted the distribution toward more positive epistasis values, and the highest epistasis values (mean and max) were found for double mutants that result in zero disrupted base pairs because the two mutations together create a new Watson-Crick or GU Wobble pair.
evidence: This is supported by the violin plot analysis shown in Figures 1-5, panel C.

claim: The highest epistasis values (mean and max) were found for double mutants that result in zero disrupted base pairs because the two mutations together create a new Watson-Crick or GU Wobble pair.
source: For all ribozymes, the analysis revealed a clear trend. On average, disrupting two base pairs resulted in negative epistasis (mean of distribution), disrupting one base pair shifted the distribution toward more positive epistasis values, and the highest epistasis values (mean and max) were found for double mutants that result in zero disrupted base pairs because the two mutations together create a new Watson-Crick or GU Wobble pair.
evidence: This is supported by the violin plot analysis shown in Figures 1-5, panel C.

claim: This trend was observed for paired regions in every ribozyme, and in all cases the distributions were significantly different (p<0.05–0.001, Mann-Whitney U test).
source: This trend was observed for paired regions in every ribozyme, and in all cases the distributions were significantly different (p<0.05–0.001, Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the epistasis data.

claim: Short-paired regions showed the largest differences in the distributions of epistatic effects for on-diagonal and off-diagonal double mutants.
source: Short-paired regions showed the largest differences in the distributions of epistatic effects for on-diagonal and off-diagonal double mutants, while longer-paired regions showed small differences in these distributions.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Longer-paired regions showed small differences in the distributions of epistatic effects for on-diagonal and off-diagonal double mutants.
source: Short-paired regions showed the largest differences in the distributions of epistatic effects for on-diagonal and off-diagonal double mutants, while longer-paired regions showed small differences in these distributions.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Short-paired regions P3 in CPEB3 and HDV (3 bp), and T1 in the twister (4 bp) showed very large differences in the mean of the distributions.
source: For example, short-paired regions P3 in CPEB3 and HDV (3 bp), and T1 in the twister (4 bp) showed very large differences in the mean of the distributions.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The largest paired region (HDV P4, 14 bp) showed a very small difference between the distribution of epistasis values found on-diagonal and off-diagonal.
source: In contrast, the largest paired region (HDV P4, 14 bp) showed a very small difference between the distribution of epistasis values found on-diagonal and off-diagonal.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Losing one base pair in HDV P4 was not deleterious to the HDV ribozyme activity under the experimental conditions.
source: This can be rationalized because losing one base pair was not deleterious to the HDV ribozyme activity under our experimental conditions (Figure 2), and this does not allow for positive epistasis upon a second mutation.
evidence: This is supported by the activity data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The effects of mutations, and their additivity, have been shown to be dependent on the local thermodynamics of the structured region.
source: Taken together, the results are consistent with other observations in both RNA and proteins, where it has been observed that the effects of mutations, and their additivity, have been shown to be dependent on the local thermodynamics of the structured region (Kraut et al., 2003; Moody and Bevilacqua, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on the thermodynamic dependence of mutational effects.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between the median deleterious effects of single mutations and the minimum free energy of the paired regions.
source: We found a significant negative correlation between the median deleterious effects of single mutations and the minimum free energy of the paired regions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Self-cleaving ribozymes often utilize a concerted acid-base catalysis mechanism where specific nucleobases act as proton donors (acid) or acceptors (base).
source: Self-cleaving ribozymes often utilize a concerted acid-base catalysis mechanism where specific nucleobases act as proton donors (acid) or acceptors (base) (Jimenez et al., 2015), and mutations at these positions abolish activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on ribozyme catalytic mechanisms.

claim: Mutations at catalytic positions abolish activity.
source: Self-cleaving ribozymes often utilize a concerted acid-base catalysis mechanism where specific nucleobases act as proton donors (acid) or acceptors (base) (Jimenez et al., 2015), and mutations at these positions abolish activity.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the importance of catalytic residues.

claim: Comprehensive pairwise mutations can potentially distinguish between catalytic residues that cannot be rescued by a second mutation, and structurally important nucleotides that can be rescued (positive epistasis).
source: Comprehensive pairwise mutations, on the other hand, can potentially distinguish between catalytic residues that cannot be rescued by a second mutation, and structurally important nucleotides that can be rescued (positive epistasis).
evidence: This is an inference about the potential of comprehensive pairwise mutation analysis.

claim: The catalytic cytosines of the CPEB3 (C57) and HDV (C75) act as proton donors due to perturbed pKa values.
source: The catalytic cytosines of the CPEB3 (C57) and HDV (C75) act as proton donors due to perturbed pKa values (Nakano et al., 2000; Skilandat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing these catalytic residues.

claim: For the twister ribozyme, the guanosine at position G39 acts as a general base, and the adenosine at position A1 acts as a general acid.
source: For the twister ribozyme (Figure 3), the guanosine at position G39 acts as a general base, and the adenosine at position A1 acts as a general acid (Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study characterizing the catalytic mechanism of the twister ribozyme.

claim: The catalytic nucleotides for the Hammerhead ribozyme are the Guanosines located at positions G25 and G39.
source: The catalytic nucleotides for the Hammerhead ribozyme (Figure 5) are the Guanosines located at positions G25 and G39 (Scott et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study identifying the catalytic residues of the hammerhead ribozyme.

claim: The hairpin ribozyme contains catalytic nucleotides at positions G29 and A59.
source: The hairpin ribozyme (Figure 4) contains catalytic nucleotides at positions G29 and A59 (Wilson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study identifying the catalytic residues of the hairpin ribozyme.

claim: In the RA heatmaps, the columns and rows associated with catalytic nucleotides result in low activity values.
source: In the RA heatmaps, the columns and rows associated with these nucleotides result in low activity values (Figures 1—5, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the heatmap data shown in Figures 1-5 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: There are no possible compensatory mutations for catalytic residues in this data set.
source: It is important to note that because there is complete coverage of all double mutants in this data set, we can be certain that there are no possible compensatory mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comprehensive coverage of double mutants in the data.

claim: Ribozymes with mutations to nucleotides found in terminal loops that are not involved in tertiary structure elements showed high RA for most single and double mutants, and essentially no epistasis.
source: Ribozymes with mutations to nucleotides found in terminal loops that are not involved in tertiary structure elements showed high RA for most single and double mutants, and essentially no epistasis.
evidence: This is supported by the data for terminal loops shown in the results section.

claim: L4 of CPEB3, L4 of HDV, and L1 and L3 of the hairpin ribozyme are terminal loops on the periphery of the ribozyme not involved in structural contacts with other nucleotides.
source: This is not surprising if these loops reside on the periphery of the ribozyme and are not involved in structural contacts with other nucleotides. This is the case for L4 of CPEB3 (Figure 1), L4 of HDV (Figure 2), and L1 and L3 of the hairpin ribozyme (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational data and structural knowledge.

claim: The internal loops LA and LB of the hairpin ribozyme are structurally important.
source: The internal loops LA and LB of the hairpin ribozyme are structurally important (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the mutational data and structural information.

claim: Interactions between nucleotides within LB include six non-Watson-Crick base-pairing interactions that are important for the formation of an active ribozyme structure.
source: Interactions between nucleotides within LB include six non-Watson-Crick base-pairing interactions that are important for the formation of an active ribozyme structure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural information shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several non-canonical base-base and sugar-base hydrogen bonds between nucleotides within LA are important for the formation of the active site.
source: Several non-canonical base-base and sugar-base hydrogen bonds between nucleotides within LA are also important for the formation of the active site (Fedor, 2000; Wilson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing the hairpin ribozyme structure.

claim: Docking between LA and LB is necessary for the formation of a catalytically active ribozyme and is facilitated by a Watson-Crick base pair between nucleotides numbered G1 and C46.
source: Docking between LA and LB is necessary for the formation of a catalytically active ribozyme and is facilitated by a Watson-Crick base pair between nucleotides numbered G1 and C46 in the version of the ribozyme used here (Rupert and Ferré-D'Amaré, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study characterizing the hairpin ribozyme structure.

claim: Most single mutations within LA and LB resulted in low self-cleavage activity.
source: In contrast to terminal loop regions, most single mutations within LA and LB resulted in low self-cleavage activity in our data (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the activity data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The double mutants within and between loop A and loop B show several instances of strong positive epistasis.
source: In addition, the double mutants within and between loop A and loop B show several instances of strong positive epistasis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), and the distributions of epistasis within and between these loops are significantly different than the terminal loops that are not structurally important (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the epistasis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4D.

claim: The distributions of epistasis within and between loop A and loop B are significantly different than the terminal loops that are not structurally important.
source: In addition, the double mutants within and between loop A and loop B show several instances of strong positive epistasis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), and the distributions of epistasis within and between these loops are significantly different than the terminal loops that are not structurally important (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical comparison shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The double mutant G1C and C46G shows strong epistasis suggesting that swapping a C-G base pair for the G-C base pair can restore activity by facilitating docking between the two loops.
source: For example, the double mutant G1C and C46G shows strong epistasis suggesting that swapping a C-G base pair for the G-C base pair can restore activity by facilitating docking between the two loops.
evidence: This is an inference based on the epistasis data and structural knowledge.

claim: Crystal structures of the sTRSV ribozyme show a base pair between the nucleotides corresponding to the nucleotides numbered here as C20 and G25 in the ribozyme construct used for the experiments.
source: Crystal structures of the sTRSV ribozyme show a base pair between the nucleotides corresponding to the nucleotides numbered here as C20 and G25 in the ribozyme construct used for our experiments (Chi et al., 2008; Martick and Scott, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structure studies.

claim: C20 and G25 showed strong positive epistasis for the mutations C20G and G25C, which substitutes a G:C base pair for the original C:G base pair.
source: These two nucleotides showed strong positive epistasis for the mutations C20G and G25C, which substitutes a G:C base pair for the original C:G base pair.
evidence: This is supported by the epistasis data for the hammerhead ribozyme.

claim: All other single and double mutants in the CUGA turn region showed low activity, and no instances of strong positive epistasis within or between this motif.
source: All other single and double mutants in this region showed low activity, and no instances of strong positive epistasis within or between this motif (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Type III hammerhead ribozymes contain tertiary interactions between nucleotides in the loops of P1 and P2 that are implicated in structural organization of the catalytic core.
source: Type III hammerhead ribozymes, like the one used in this study, contain tertiary interactions between nucleotides in the loops of P1 and P2 that are implicated in structural organization of the catalytic core.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Type III hammerhead ribozymes.

claim: A crystal structure of the loop-loop interaction in hammerhead ribozyme showed a network of interhelical non-canonical base pairs and stacks, with several nucleobases in stem-loop I interacting with more than one nucleobase in stem-loop II.
source: A crystal structure of this loop-loop interaction showed a network of interhelical non-canonical base pairs and stacks, with several nucleobases in stem-loop I interacting with more than one nucleobase in stem-loop II (Chi et al., 2008; Martick and Scott, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structure studies.

claim: There are numerous different loop sequences in naturally occurring hammerhead ribozymes indicating that this loop-loop interaction can be formed by a variety of different sequences.
source: However, there are numerous different loop sequences in naturally occurring hammerhead ribozymes indicating that this loop-loop interaction can be formed by a variety of different sequences (Burke and Greathouse, 2005; Perreault et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies analyzing natural hammerhead ribozyme sequences.

claim: Most individual and double mutations in the hammerhead loop regions do not reduce activity.
source: Surprisingly, however, we found that most individual and double mutations do not reduce activity (Figure 5), and double mutants do not show positive epistasis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The multiple interactions between the loops compensate for mutations that break a single interaction.
source: This indicates that the multiple interactions between the loops compensate for mutations that break a single interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutational data.

claim: The mutational robustness of the hammerhead loops has been exploited in bioengineering applications, where insertion of an aptamer into one of the loops and randomization of the other allowed for the selection of synthetic riboswitches.
source: It is interesting to note that the mutational robustness of these loops has been exploited in bioengineering applications, where insertion of an aptamer into one of the loops and randomization of the other allowed for the selection of synthetic riboswitches (Townshend et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study developing synthetic riboswitches.

claim: There is support for a two-nucleotide T1 pseudoknot in CPEB3 involving a non-canonical U-U base pair.
source: We also find support for a two-nucleotide T1 pseudoknot in CPEB3 involving a non-canonical U-U base pair.
evidence: This is supported by the mutational data for CPEB3.

claim: The U:U base pair in CPEB3 T1 has been confirmed and implicated as a magnesium binding site based on NMR and Tb3+ cleavage data.
source: While no crystal structure of the CPEB3 ribozyme has been solved, this U:U base pair has been confirmed and implicated as a magnesium binding site based on NMR and Tb3+ cleavage data (Skilandat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study characterizing the CPEB3 structure.

claim: G:C and C:G base pairs can support activity in the CPEB3 T1 pseudoknot.
source: In our data, we find that G:C and C:G base pairs can support activity.
evidence: This is supported by the mutational data for CPEB3.

claim: Every single and double mutant was observed for all ribozymes in each replicate, indicating 100% coverage of these mutant classes for all data sets.
source: We observed every single and double mutant for all ribozymes in each replicate, indicating 100% coverage of these mutant classes for all of our data sets.

source: The HDV data showed the lowest depth, possibly because it is a larger ribozyme (87 nt), and fewer reads mapped to the single and double mutants (Table 1).

source: For example, all pairwise mutations in a 42-nucleotide region of the same twister ribozyme were previously reported (Kobori and Yokobayashi, 2016).

source: The pairwise epistasis analysis presented here adds an additional approach to extract information from such high-throughput sequencing-based analysis of self-cleaving ribozymes.

source: Unlike the rescue analysis, which can only identify positive interactions, the ability to detect negative epistatic interactions may help further identify structurally important regions for RNA sequence design and engineering efforts.

claim: The comprehensiveness of the double mutants enabled identification of catalytic residues.
source: In addition, the comprehensiveness of the double mutants enabled identification of catalytic residues.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of catalytic residues in the results section.

claim: Recently, there has been significant progress toward predicting RNA structures from sequence using machine learning approaches.
source: Recently, there has been significant progress toward predicting RNA structures from sequence using machine learning approaches (Calonaci et al., 2020; Townshend et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent machine learning studies.

claim: Machine learning models for RNA structure prediction are typically trained on structural biology data from x-ray crystallography, chemical probing (SHAPE), and natural sequence conservation.
source: The machine learning models are typically trained on structural biology data from x-ray crystallography, chemical probing (SHAPE), and natural sequence conservation.
evidence: This describes the typical training data for machine learning models.

claim: The approach used in this study is similar to SHAPE in that it can be obtained with common lab equipment and commercially available reagents.
source: Our approach is similar to SHAPE in that it can be obtained with common lab equipment and commercially available reagents.
evidence: This is a comparison of the experimental approach to SHAPE.

claim: The activity data presented provides information similar to natural sequence conservation, except that it provides quantitative effects of mutations, not just frequency.
source: The activity data presented provides information similar to natural sequence conservation, except that it provides quantitative effects of mutations, not just frequency.
evidence: This is a comparison of the data type to natural sequence conservation.

claim: The comparative approach based on covarying nucleotide positions may not be able to identify important nucleotides or structural elements other than canonical base pairs.
source: However, this 'comparative approach' may not be able to identify important nucleotides or structural elements other than canonical base pairs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the limitations of comparative sequence analysis.

claim: The activity-based data presented will provide information not present in other training data sets and help advance computational predictions.
source: We hope that the activity-based data presented here will provide information not present in these other training data sets and help advance computational predictions.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential impact of the data.

claim: Single-stranded DNA molecules used as templates for in vitro transcription were synthesized using doped oligos containing 97% of the base of the reference sequence and 1% of the three other remaining bases at each position.
source: Single-stranded DNA molecules used as templates for in vitro transcription were synthesized as described previously (Kobori and Yokobayashi, 2016), using doped oligos containing 97% of the base of the reference sequence and 1% of the three other remaining bases at each position (Keck Oligo Synthesis Resource, Yale).
evidence: This describes the library synthesis method used in the study.

claim: A constant structured RNA cassette was appended to the template sequences to provide a reverse transcription primer binding site.
source: A constant structured RNA cassette was appended to the template sequences to provide a reverse transcription primer binding site (Wilkinson et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes a technical aspect of the experimental design.

claim: The co-transcriptional self-cleavage reactions were carried out in triplicate.
source: The co-transcriptional self-cleavage reactions were carried out in triplicate by combining 20 μL 10× T7 transcription buffer (500 μL 1 M Tris pH 7.5, 50 μL 1 M DTT, 20 μL 1 M Spermidine, 150 μL 1 M MgCl2, 280 μL RNase-free water), 4 μL rNTP (25 mM, NEB, Ipswich, Ma), 8 μL T7 RNA Polymerase-Plus enzyme mix (1600 U, Invitrogen, Waltham, MA), 160 μL nuclease-free water, and 8 μL of double-stranded DNA template (4 pmol, 0.5 μM PCR product) at 37°C for 30 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental replication strategy.

claim: Reverse transcription was carried out using a 5′ RACE protocol using phased template switching oligos.
source: Reverse transcription was carried out using a 5′ RACE protocol using phased template switching oligo's (TSO1-4, Supplementary file 1) as described previously (Bendixsen et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the reverse transcription method used.

claim: Four different template switching oligos (TSO 1–4) with different lengths and nucleotide compositions were used such that the first nucleotides read during sequencing are a balance of all four nucleotides, and the ribozymes are sequenced in four different frames relative to the primer.
source: Four different template switching oligos (TSO 1–4) with different lengths and nucleotide compositions were used such that the first nucleotides read during sequencing are a balance of all four nucleotides, and the ribozymes are sequenced in four different frames relative to the primer.
evidence: This describes a technical aspect of the sequencing strategy.

claim: A unique index combination was assigned to each ribozyme and for each replicate.
source: A unique index combination was assigned to each ribozyme and for each replicate.
evidence: This describes the indexing strategy for multiplexed sequencing.

claim: Paired-end sequencing reads were obtained for the pooled libraries using an Illumina HiSeq 4000.
source: Paired-end sequencing reads were obtained for the pooled libraries using an Illumina HiSeq 4000 (Genomics and Cell Characterization Core Facility, University of Oregon).
evidence: This describes the sequencing platform used.

claim: Paired-end sequencing reads were joined using FLASh, allowing 'outies' due to overlapping reads.
source: Paired-end sequencing reads were joined using FLASh, allowing 'outies' due to overlapping reads.
evidence: This describes the bioinformatic processing of sequencing reads.

claim: The joined sequencing reads were analyzed using custom Julia scripts.
source: The joined sequencing reads were analyzed using custom Julia scripts available at https://gitlab.com/bsu/biocompute-public/mut_12 (Beck, 2023).
evidence: This describes the computational analysis approach.

claim: Values greater than 1 indicate positive epistasis, and values less than 0 indicate negative epistasis.
source: Values greater than 1 indicate positive epistasis, and values less than 0 indicate negative epistasis.
evidence: This defines the interpretation of epistasis values.

claim: Mann-Whitney U test was used to determine the probability that epistasis or activity values of different structural elements were from the same distribution.
source: Mann-Whitney U test was used to determine the probability that epistasis or activity values of different structural elements were from the same distribution.
evidence: This describes the statistical test used for comparisons.
